course.name: AI Internal Audit & Data Analytics Course
course.tagline: Run a municipal internal audit under the MFMA and the Global Internal Audit Standards, from the annual cycle to Audit Committee reporting, and know why every control exists.
course.summary: The AI Internal Audit & Data Analytics Platform supports municipal internal audit: a Standards & Legislation library that loads and pins criteria, the twelve-stage workflow in three bands, independence and competency, analytics and evidence, findings with cited criteria and MFMA s32 classification, reporting and conformance, follow-up including Auditor-General findings, and controls over AI-assisted content. This course explains the concepts, roles and controls behind those features for everyone who uses the platform, from staff auditors to the Municipal Manager, the Audit Committee and IT administrators.

lessons.title: Orientation: Roles, Municipal Terms and Signing In
lessons.subtitle: Who does what, what each role sees, and how you get in
lessons.overview: The platform serves eight roles: Staff / Senior Auditor, Audit Manager / Director, Head of Internal Audit (CAE), Process Owner / Auditee, Executive Management, Municipal Manager (accounting officer), Audit Committee and IT & System Administrator. It speaks the municipality's language rather than the Standards': where the IIA Global Internal Audit Standards say board, the screens say Audit Committee; senior management is the Municipal Manager; the chief audit executive is the Head of Internal Audit (the role key stays cae). One Audit Committee member is flagged as chair, and only the chair records the Committee's decisions. Roles carry explicit permissions, seniority confers nothing beyond them, and the server enforces every one: a record outside your scope answers as if it does not exist, and the menu shows only the pages your role can use.
keyPoints: Scopes: auditors see the engagements they are assigned to, audit managers those they manage, the Head of Internal Audit all internal audit content, process owners their own department's findings from approval onwards, executives and the Municipal Manager approved findings and actions, and the Audit Committee reported findings.
The Municipal Manager accepts the charter and the audit plan after the Audit Committee chair approves them; acceptance is what brings a version into force.
The Audit Committee chair is designated with Make chair by the Head of Internal Audit or the IT administrator; there is one active chair at a time.
The IT & System Administrator manages users, access and the audit trail and sees no audit content.
A super user may configure settings within its own role's domain only; it gains no approval authority and no evidence access.

Accounts are issued, never self-registered; a temporary password must be changed at first sign-in and expires after 72 hours. Auditor, audit manager, Head of Internal Audit, IT administrator and super-user accounts need a second person's approval.
Two-factor sign-in is required for the Head of Internal Audit, audit managers and IT administrators in a customer installation; five failed passwords or codes lock the account for 15 minutes.
Home pages differ: My work for process owners, the Executive Dashboard for the audit team, executives, the Municipal Manager and the Audit Committee, the Audit Trail for an IT administrator.
operationalProcedures: 1. Sign in on the Sign in page with your Email address and Password (usernames are not accepted).
2. At a first sign-in with a temporary password, choose your own password; nothing else opens until you do.
3. If your role requires it, set up two-factor sign-in from the QR code and keep the ten recovery codes safe.
4. Land on your home page and check the status line: Live, or Cached as of.
5. Open My work and the Notifications bell for everything awaiting you, and Help & Training for the guide written for your role.
takeaways: If a page or record is missing, the cause is usually your role or scope, not a fault.
Only the Audit Committee chair records the Committee's approvals; another member is refused.
Being a super user never lets you approve anything your role cannot already approve.

quiz.question: On screen, what does the platform call the Standards' "chief audit executive"?
options: The Municipal Manager
The Audit Committee chair
The Head of Internal Audit
The accounting officer
quiz.explanation: The municipal terms replace the Standards' terms: the chief audit executive is shown as the Head of Internal Audit (the role key stays cae).

quiz.question: An Audit Committee member who is not the chair chooses Approve plan. What happens?
options: The step is refused: only the chair records the Committee's decision
The plan is approved and the chair is notified
The plan comes into force immediately
The approval waits for a second member
quiz.explanation: Only the Audit Committee chair approves or returns the charter and plan; other members are refused.

quiz.question: What does being a super user add to a role?
options: The right to approve findings the role could not otherwise approve
Read access to all evidence files
The ability to issue accounts for any role
Configuration of settings within that role's own domain, and nothing else
quiz.explanation: Super users configure within their own role's domain and gain no approval authority or evidence access.

lessons.title: Standards, Legislation and the Twelve Stages
lessons.subtitle: The library every engagement cites, and how the workflow is built on it
lessons.overview: Municipal internal audit answers to two bodies of rules at once: the IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024) and South African law, led by the Municipal Finance Management Act (MFMA). The Standards & legislation page holds both as seeded, versioned records rather than hard-coded lists. Standards are listed by domain and principle with numbers and titles only, because the IIA owns the text. Legislation, frameworks and guidance carry their citation, the provisions loaded as criteria, the audit areas they apply to, their status and effective dates, so the library can say exactly which law applies to an audit area on a given date. The same library maps every one of the twelve workflow stages to its standards, its South African trigger and its gate.
keyPoints: The twelve stages sit in three bands: Once a year: set up the function (1 Mandate and charter, 2 Ethics and independence, 3 Audit universe and risk assessment, 4 Strategy and annual plan); For every audit engagement (5 Engagement planning, 6 Fieldwork, 7 Findings and conclusions, 8 Supervision and review, 9 Engagement reporting, 10 Follow-up); Every quarter and every year: oversight (11 Audit Committee and council reporting, 12 Quality assurance and improvement).

Examples of South African triggers: MFMA s165 (internal audit unit and the risk-based plan), MFMA s32 (unauthorised, irregular, fruitless and wasteful expenditure), MFMA s131 (Auditor-General issues), MFMA s166 (the Audit Committee), the Performance Regulations reg 14, and MFMA Circular 65 (external assessment at least every five years).
Instruments carry a status (In force, Not yet in operation, Superseded) and effective dates; Criteria for an audit area on a date shows what planning would load and what is Not applied, and why.
The Public Procurement Act 28 of 2024 is not applied while it is not in operation, and King IV applies only to financial years before King V.
Audit areas such as Supply chain and contract management, Revenue, rates and debtors, Performance information or ICT, information and records select the legislation that loads at engagement planning.
The six IIA Topical Requirements are listed with status and effective date: mandatory for assurance engagements once in effect, recommended for advisory engagements and before that date.

Only the Head of Internal Audit maintains the library: every edit is a new version, every record has an owner and a yearly review, and the review queue lists overdue reviews and records with no owner.
The seven Items to confirm (for example the IIA licence and whether the Public Procurement Act is in operation) stay open until the municipality answers them; they are never guessed.
operationalProcedures: 1. Open Standards & legislation and read the Standards tab by domain and principle.
2. On Legislation filter by Audit area and Status, and use Criteria for an audit area on a date for the area you will audit.
3. On Topical Requirements read each status and effective date.
4. On Workflow stages read each stage's standards, legislation, South African trigger and gate.
5. Head of Internal Audit: on Review assign owners, choose Mark reviewed, and use Edit, Add local instrument or Mark superseded with a reason.
takeaways: Law applies by date: an instrument not in operation or superseded before the planned start does not load.
The product shows IIA numbers and titles only; full text needs the client's own IIA licence.
A library edit never rewrites the past: it is a new version, and engagements already approved keep what they pinned.

quiz.question: Why does the Standards tab show only numbers and titles?
options: The text is still being translated
The IIA owns the text; it is entered only under the client's own licence
The text is shown only to the Audit Committee
Titles are enough for the assistant
quiz.explanation: Standards records keep their text empty unless the Head of Internal Audit enters it under the organisation's own IIA licence.

quiz.question: Which band does stage 11, Audit Committee and council reporting, belong to?
options: Every quarter and every year: oversight
Once a year: set up the function
For every audit engagement
It has no band
quiz.explanation: Stages 11 and 12 form the oversight band; stages 1 to 4 are annual and 5 to 10 run for every engagement.

quiz.question: An instrument is Not yet in operation on an engagement's planned start. What does planning do with it?
options: Loads it with a warning
Loads it and marks it superseded
Asks the Audit Committee to decide
Does not load it; the criteria check lists it as not applied
quiz.explanation: Only instruments in force on the date load; the rest are listed as not applied with the reason.

lessons.title: Governance: Charter, Plan, Coverage and the Annual Cycle
lessons.subtitle: Stages 1 to 4: approved by the chair, accepted by the Municipal Manager
lessons.overview: The internal audit charter and the risk-based audit plan are versioned records. The Head of Internal Audit drafts a version and submits it to the Audit Committee; the chair approves it or returns it with a note; and the Municipal Manager, as accounting officer, accepts it. An approved version is not yet in force: it comes into force only on acceptance, and the version it replaces stays in force until that moment and is superseded in the same step. Before a plan goes to the Committee it is checked for coverage against the seven areas of MFMA s165(2)(b) and the risk register, and the universe it is drawn from links each auditable unit to its risks, the IDP, the SDBIP, prior Auditor-General findings and other assurance providers. Together these make up stages 1 to 4, the annual cycle, which must be complete before a year's engagements may start fieldwork.
keyPoints: Charter and plan steps: Submit to the Audit Committee (Head of Internal Audit), Approve plan or Approve charter / Return plan or Return charter with a note (chair only), Accept plan or Accept charter with an optional note (Municipal Manager), Amend (new version) with a reason.
Segregation of duties: the person who prepared or approved a version cannot accept it; the Municipal Manager cannot decline in this release.
Amendment is refused while another version is in draft, submitted or awaiting acceptance.

The seven s165(2)(b) areas: internal audit, internal controls, accounting procedures and practices, risk and risk management, performance management, loss control, and compliance with the MFMA, DoRA and other legislation. An area with no planned item is a Gap; a high or critical risk with no planned item is Not covered.
Plan items carry hours, an optional Estimated cost (rand), their s165(2)(b) areas and audit areas; a plan version carries a budget in rand.

Stage 1 and stage 4 are computed (charter in force and within its review date, 12 months after acceptance by default; the year's plan approved and accepted). Stages 2 and 3 are sign-offs by the Head of Internal Audit: Sign off the declarations and Sign off the risk assessment.
Each stage locks the next, a plan for a year is submitted only after that year's stage 3 sign-off, and fieldwork needs the complete cycle of the financial year of the planned start.
operationalProcedures: 1. Head of Internal Audit: open Plan & charter, choose Amend (new version), edit the draft and check Coverage.
2. Choose Submit to the Audit Committee.
3. Chair: choose Approve plan or Return plan (or the charter equivalents) from My work → Awaiting your approval.
4. Municipal Manager: open My work → Awaiting your acceptance and choose Accept plan or Accept charter.
5. Head of Internal Audit: on Workflow stages → Annual cycle sign off stages 2 and 3 and confirm that stages 1 and 4 are complete.
takeaways: Approved is not in force: until the Municipal Manager accepts, the previous version governs.
Read Coverage before submitting; gaps are flagged, not fixed for you.
An incomplete annual cycle stops every engagement of that year at Start fieldwork.

quiz.question: The Audit Committee chair has approved plan version 3. Which version is in force?
options: Version 3, from the moment of approval
No version until the next financial year
The previous version, until the Municipal Manager accepts version 3
Both versions together
quiz.explanation: Approval leaves the version approved but not in force; acceptance brings it into force and supersedes the old one in the same step.

quiz.question: What must be signed off before a plan for a year can be submitted to the Audit Committee?
options: Stage 3 (audit universe and risk assessment) of that year
The quality programme of the previous year
Every engagement of the previous year
The Municipal Manager's acceptance of the plan
quiz.explanation: plan.submit needs at least one first-year item and stage 3 of that year signed off by the Head of Internal Audit.

quiz.question: Coverage shows "Loss control: Gap". What does that mean?
options: A loss was found in the audit
The area has too many planned items
The Municipal Manager has not accepted the plan
No planned item in that year covers that s165(2)(b) area
quiz.explanation: A Gap is one of the seven s165(2)(b) areas with no planned item.

lessons.title: Independence and Competency
lessons.subtitle: Declarations, CPD, impairments and the conflict check on every engagement
lessons.overview: Objectivity is a precondition of the work, so the platform turns it into records the workflow checks. Every auditor, audit manager and the Head of Internal Audit signs an annual declaration for the municipal financial year (July to June): the code of conduct for municipal staff, objectivity statements and a confidentiality undertaking. The register also holds qualifications, CPD hours against a target, prior roles in the municipality and impairments to objectivity. On every engagement each team member, the manager included, records a conflict check. These records are personal information: the details are visible only to the auditor and the Head of Internal Audit, and the Audit Committee chair sees counts and names only.
keyPoints: Without a declaration for the current financial year, or with an open impairment concerning the engagement, its department or one of its audit areas, assignment to an engagement team is refused.

A prior role in the department or area that ended within 12 months of the planned start raises an independence warning (Standards 2.1, 2.2); only the Head of Internal Audit can proceed, with a reason kept on the engagement.
The CPD target is a workflow setting, 40 hours per financial year by default (a product default, not from a source).
Declarations for the coming year can be signed from 1 April (three months before it starts, a product default); signing again creates a new version that is acknowledged again.
The Head of Internal Audit acknowledges declarations and resolves impairments; the Audit Committee chair acknowledges the Head of Internal Audit's own declaration. Nobody acknowledges their own.
A declared conflict on an engagement opens an impairment automatically and notifies the Head of Internal Audit and the manager; colleagues see only that a conflict was declared.
Start fieldwork needs every team member's conflict check and no open impairment concerning the engagement. Stage 2 of the annual cycle needs every register member declared and acknowledged.
operationalProcedures: 1. Open Independence & competency and choose Sign this year's declaration.
2. Log CPD with its date, hours, activity and provider, and add your qualifications.
3. Disclose an impairment if one arises; it stays open until the Head of Internal Audit resolves it.
4. On each engagement you join, choose Record my conflict check on Overview → Team independence.
5. Head of Internal Audit: on Register, Open each auditor to Acknowledge, Resolve or Record a prior role.
takeaways: No declaration, no assignment.
A conflict check is per engagement, not per year.
Independence details are personal information; the Committee sees counts and names only.

quiz.question: A manager tries to add an auditor who has no declaration for the current year. What happens?
options: The auditor is added with a warning
The assignment is refused until the auditor declares
The auditor is added and the Committee is notified
The Head of Internal Audit is asked to declare for them
quiz.explanation: Assignment is refused without a declaration for the current financial year.

quiz.question: An auditor's prior role in the department ended eight months before the planned start. Who can confirm the assignment?
options: The engagement's audit manager
The Audit Committee chair
Only the Head of Internal Audit, with a recorded reason
Nobody; it is always refused
quiz.explanation: A prior role ending within 12 months is a warning only the Head of Internal Audit can confirm, with a reason kept on the engagement.

quiz.question: Who acknowledges the Head of Internal Audit's own declaration?
options: The Municipal Manager
Nobody in this release
Any audit manager
The Audit Committee chair
quiz.explanation: Nobody acknowledges their own; the chair acknowledges the Head of Internal Audit's declaration.

lessons.title: Analytics, Evidence and Sampling
lessons.subtitle: Whole populations, candidate cases, vouching and reproducible samples
lessons.overview: Instead of testing only a sample, the platform runs analytics rules over whole transaction populations, grouped into Procurement & SCM, Disbursements & AP, Payroll & HR and General Ledger. What a rule raises is a case: a candidate for an auditor's review, never a finding. Populations arrive through governed imports that keep the file exactly as received with its SHA-256, validate it with control totals and record on every row the file and row it came from. Supporting documents are uploaded as evidence and, where readable, their invoice fields are extracted and matched to payments; every item that is not a clean match goes to an exception queue that a person decides with a reason. Where a test needs a sample, the drawn sample records its seed and the population's fingerprint, so it can be reproduced, and the working paper records that sample as its sample basis.
keyPoints: Example rules: split orders below a threshold, vendor–employee conflicts (shared bank account, address or director ID number), duplicate payments, dormant vendor reactivation, Benford's law on first digits, shared bank accounts in payroll, no leave and no deductions, paid after termination, excessive overtime, weekend and after-hours journals, round-amount journals and manual journals by unusual users.
Thresholds such as procurement or overtime limits are configurable rule parameters chosen for the demonstration, not statutory values; they must be confirmed against the municipality's own policies.
Case statuses are flagged, under review, confirmed, cleared and escalated. In this release a status cannot be set directly; linking a case to a draft finding moves it to under review.
Re-running analytics updates cases whose details changed and never changes a status a reviewer set.
Imports accept CSV and Excel (.xlsx). Macro-enabled workbooks, legacy .xls and password-protected files are refused; formulas are not calculated and links to other files are not followed.
Vouching outcomes are matched, partially matched, duplicate suspect and unmatched, with which details agreed.

Decisions on the exception queue: Confirm (a reason unless it is a clean match), Correct a value (with a reason; the value as read is kept beside the correction and the item is matched again) or Record an exception (with a reason).
Invoice extraction is rule-based, not AI; text recognition of scans and images is not available in this release, so images and PowerPoint files are stored only.
Samples use simple random, systematic or monetary unit selection; a working paper links its sample under Sample drawn in the platform, which fills the size, population and selection.
operationalProcedures: 1. Open Imports, upload the file, map the columns, choose Validate, then Commit N rows and Run analytics.
2. Open an analytics module or Cases, choose Show these on a rule, and read a case's explanation and records.
3. Open Evidence & Vouching, choose Upload and extract, and decide each exception with Confirm, Correct a value or Record an exception.
4. Open Samples for tests, choose the Test, Population, Method and Sample size, and choose Draw the sample.
5. On the working paper, set the sample basis to Statistical sample and choose the sample drawn in the platform.
takeaways: A case is a question to answer, not a conclusion.
Never rely on demonstration thresholds as policy.
A correction never overwrites the value as read; it sits beside it with its reason.

quiz.question: An analytics rule flags a vendor that shares a bank account with an employee. What is that case?
options: A confirmed finding sent to the process owner
Evidence of fraud that must be escalated
An automatic control failure
A candidate for review by internal audit
quiz.explanation: Cases are candidates for review; only an approved finding states a conclusion.

quiz.question: An auditor corrects an extracted invoice amount. What happens to the original value?
options: It is kept beside the correction, and the item is matched again
It is overwritten by the correction
It is deleted after approval
It is sent to the process owner
quiz.explanation: The value as read is kept beside the correction, with the reason.

quiz.question: Why does a drawn sample record its seed and the population's SHA-256 fingerprint?
options: So it is encrypted on the device
So the process owner can approve it
So the same inputs give the same sample and a reviewer can reproduce it
So the analytics rules can re-run on it
quiz.explanation: Seed plus fingerprint make the sample reproducible evidence of method.

lessons.title: Engagement Planning: Criteria, Topical Requirements and Pinning
lessons.subtitle: Stage 5: what the engagement will be judged against, fixed at approval
lessons.overview: Every engagement is judged against evaluation criteria (Standard 13.4). The platform does not leave them to memory: the engagement's audit areas select the legislation in force on its planned start, which loads automatically as criteria; the team may deselect one with a reason or add another instrument in force from the register. The engagement is assurance (the default) or advisory, which decides whether each IIA Topical Requirement is mandatory or recommended. Every Topical Requirement must be answered; an applicable one loads its governance, risk management and control processes checklist into the programme. When the manager approves planning, the criteria, the standards of stages 5 to 10 and the Topical Requirement answers are pinned with the library version in force at that moment, so later library edits never change a performed engagement.
keyPoints: Submit planning for approval needs objectives and scope, at least one risk and control in scope, a procedure linked to a risk in scope, at least one audit area and one criterion, and every Topical Requirement answered with the reasons required.
A Topical Requirement is mandatory for an assurance engagement whose planned start is on or after its effective date; otherwise recommended (a product reading to confirm).

Excluding a checklist item of a mandatory requirement, or answering Does not apply to a mandatory one whose triggers match the areas, needs a reason and Approve exclusion by the engagement's audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit, never the person who answered.
Included checklist items load as procedures linked to every risk in scope; once loaded, a procedure stays in the programme.
Approve planning pins the criteria (criteria snapshot); the tab then shows Pinned when planning was approved and marks "a newer version exists" after a library edit.
Changing the objectives, scope, risks, controls, programme, criteria or answers after approval voids it; the next approval pins again.
Planning also records the notification letter and entrance meeting, and every team member's conflict check, before Start fieldwork.
operationalProcedures: 1. On Planning criteria choose Edit under Areas and type and set the audit areas and engagement type.
2. Read the Auto criteria; Deselect with a reason or Add from register as needed.
3. Choose Answer on each Topical Requirement; include or exclude checklist items with reasons and Save answer.
4. Supervisor: choose Approve exclusion where one awaits approval.
5. Team: Submit planning for approval; manager: Approve planning.
takeaways: Criteria come from the library by area and date; the auditor's job is to confirm, deselect or add with reasons.
The person who answers a Topical Requirement never approves its exclusion.
What was approved is what the engagement is judged against, whatever the library says later.

quiz.question: A Topical Requirement took effect before an advisory engagement's planned start. Is it mandatory?
options: Yes, because it is in effect
No; for an advisory engagement it is recommended
Only if the Audit Committee says so
Only for engagements in the ICT area
quiz.explanation: Mandatory applies to assurance engagements on or after the effective date; advisory engagements are recommended.

quiz.question: The library entry for an instrument is edited after an engagement's planning was approved. What happens to the engagement?
options: Its criteria update to the new version
Its planning approval is voided
Nothing changes; its pinned version stays and the tab marks that a newer version exists
The engagement returns to planning
quiz.explanation: Approval pins the criteria with the version in force then; a library edit does not void the approval.

quiz.question: Who may approve an exclusion from a mandatory Topical Requirement?
options: The engagement's audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit, not the person who answered
Any member of the engagement team
The Municipal Manager
The person who recorded the answer
quiz.explanation: Segregation of duties rule topical.exclusion: someone other than the answerer, who is the supervisor.

lessons.title: Fieldwork, Review, Quality Assurance and Gate Overrides
lessons.subtitle: Stages 6 and 8: what each gate checks, and the one controlled way past it
lessons.overview: An engagement moves through planning, fieldwork, review, quality assurance, reporting, follow-up and closed. Each move is guarded by a gate that the server checks: the same check that decides whether a button is offered enforces the step, so a blocked step shows its reasons. Fieldwork is documented in working papers, each tied to the programme step it documents, with evidence, a recorded sample basis and the standards it evidences. Approvals are bound to the exact content they approved, so a later change voids them visibly. When a gate blocks for a reason the function accepts, there is one controlled exception: a gate override, requested with a reason, decided by someone else, and good for one attempt.
keyPoints: Start fieldwork needs a team, the notification letter recorded at least the lead time before (14 days by default), the entrance meeting, approved and unchanged planning, every team member's conflict check, no open impairment, and stages 1 to 4 of the planned start's financial year complete.

Mark as prepared needs the title and summary, the programme step, at least one evidence file, the sample basis (Statistical sample, Judgemental sample, Full population or Not sampled), every open review note answered, and an AI-content review where AI-assisted.
An approval applies to one content version; a new evidence file or a changed sample basis voids it.

Complete review needs every paper approved at its current version, every note cleared, every finding approved or later and no request open. Quality assurance is an eight-item checklist completed by a manager and signed by someone who neither completed it nor prepared any working paper.

An override passes exactly the blockers it lists, on one attempt; the Head of Internal Audit decides, or the Audit Committee chair when the Head of Internal Audit asked; never the requester. Unused, it expires after 14 days (a product default).

Never overridable: segregation of duties, permissions, the chair's authority, the record's state and a named auditor's AI-content review. Management responses have no override, and closure uses a risk acceptance instead.
operationalProcedures: 1. Record each test result, write working papers with their sample basis and standards, attach evidence and choose Mark as prepared.
2. Choose Submit fieldwork for review.
3. Manager: Start review, Request changes or Approve working paper, clear notes, then Complete review.
4. Complete the QA checklist; an eligible reviewer chooses Sign quality assurance.
5. Where a gate blocks with good reason, choose Request override with a reason; the decider approves or rejects it on Workflow stages → Overrides.
takeaways: A greyed-out step always shows why; complete its blockers or request an override, never look for another route.
Editing approved content voids the approval: that is the control, not a fault.
An override is a single, recorded exception, not a waiver of the rule.

quiz.question: A working paper has its programme step and summary but no evidence file. What happens on Mark as prepared?
options: It is prepared with a warning
The reviewer is asked to attach evidence
It is prepared and the evidence is requested from the auditee
It is refused until at least one evidence file is attached
quiz.explanation: workpaper.prepare needs at least one evidence file, the programme step and the sample basis.

quiz.question: The Head of Internal Audit requests an override for their own engagement. Who decides it?
options: The Audit Committee chair
The Head of Internal Audit
The engagement's audit manager
The Municipal Manager
quiz.explanation: Nobody decides their own override; the chair decides one the Head of Internal Audit requested.

quiz.question: An AI-assisted finding has no named auditor's review. Can an override pass Submit for review?
options: Yes, with the Head of Internal Audit's approval
Yes, once, within 14 days
No; a named auditor's AI-content review is never overridable
Only if the Audit Committee chair approves
quiz.explanation: The review is a person's statement, not a condition an override can waive.

lessons.title: Findings: Cited Criteria, Root Cause, MFMA s32 and Segregation of Duties
lessons.subtitle: Stage 7: a finding that names its criteria and the money at stake
lessons.overview: A finding is written with the 5 Cs, now labelled as the municipal standard expects: Criteria, Condition, Root cause, Effect and Recommendation, with a Significance rating. It must cite at least one of the engagement's criteria, the instruments (with a provision where chosen) and standards pinned at planning, so every finding can be traced to the law or standard it measures against. Where the finding reports unauthorised, irregular, or fruitless and wasteful expenditure, it carries its MFMA s32 classification with the amount in rand, following MFMA Circular 68. A finding is approved only by a manager who did not prepare it, and the management action plan that follows must name an owner and a due date for every action.
keyPoints: Submit for review needs criteria, condition, root cause, effect and recommendation written, at least one criterion cited, and an AI-content review where the finding or its evidence is AI-assisted.
Only the engagement's criteria can be cited (pinned at approval, live before then); add an instrument to the engagement's criteria first if it is missing.
Root cause is the stored cause, Effect the stored consequence, and the Significance rating the severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low); exports and documents use the same labels.

A classified finding cites the MFMA s32 provision automatically, carries an s32 badge (filter MFMA s32), is listed on the Committee view with totals, and appears in the export columns MFMA s32 classification and UIFW amount (R).
Approve finding and Return for changes are for a manager who did not prepare it; a returned finding shows the note on the draft.
After approval, process owners are notified and the response falls due after the configured days (14 by default).
Record management response needs, unless management disagrees, at least one action, and every action with an owner and a due date.
operationalProcedures: 1. Choose New finding on the engagement's Findings tab.
2. Tick the Criteria cited and write the Criteria, Condition, Root cause, Effect and Recommendation; choose the Significance rating.
3. Set the MFMA s32 classification and Amount (R) where it applies.
4. Choose Submit for review; a manager who did not prepare it chooses Approve finding or Return for changes.
5. Process owner: Record management response with an owner and a due date on every action.
takeaways: No criterion cited, no submission.
An s32 classification is part of the finding record and of every summary built from it.
The preparer never approves their own finding.

quiz.question: A draft finding has all five fields written but cites no criterion. What happens on Submit for review?
options: It is submitted and the manager adds criteria
It is refused until at least one of the engagement's criteria is cited
It is submitted with a warning
The MFMA is cited automatically
quiz.explanation: finding.submit needs at least one of the engagement's criteria cited.

quiz.question: A finding is classified as irregular expenditure. What else does the system do?
options: Cites the MFMA s32 provision automatically
Sends the finding to the Auditor-General
Closes the finding
Raises its significance rating to Critical
quiz.explanation: A classified finding cites the s32 provision automatically, even if the engagement did not pin the MFMA.

quiz.question: Management agrees with a finding and adds one action with no due date. What happens on Record management response?
options: It is accepted and the auditor sets the date
The default due date is applied
It is accepted, but the report cannot be issued
It is refused: every action needs an owner and a due date
quiz.explanation: The response step checks that every action has an owner and a due date unless management disagrees.

lessons.title: Reporting, Conformance and the Quality Programme
lessons.subtitle: Stages 9, 11 and 12: issued reports that bind what they rest on
lessons.overview: The final engagement report is approved and issued by the Head of Internal Audit, and the issued version is frozen with a SHA-256 that binds the findings, responses, action plans, evidence and approvals, and now also the engagement conclusion and overall rating, each finding's cited criteria and s32 classification, the distribution list and the conformance statement. That statement, "conducted in conformance with the Global Internal Audit Standards", is printed only when the quality programme supports it on the day of issue; otherwise the report lists why it is withheld and never claims it. Errors found after issue are corrected by a reissue that keeps the original. Beyond each engagement, the Head of Internal Audit issues quarterly reports to the Audit Committee, quarterly performance audit reports and an annual quality report, each frozen once issued; the chair records the Committee's noting of each quarter and its yearly receipt of the quality results.
keyPoints: Approve and issue final report needs the draft approved, the exit meeting, a response and complete action plan on every finding, QA signed, the engagement conclusion and rating (Standard 14.5), the distribution list (Standard 15.1) and every AI-assisted item reviewed.

The conclusion is written by the engagement's audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit on a product default scale: Effective; Partially effective: improvement needed; Ineffective: major improvement needed.
Correct and reissue (Standard 11.4) records what was wrong, the correction, and confirmation that the distribution list was told; the superseded version is kept unchanged.

Conformance needs the latest external assessment within five years and the latest self-assessment within 12 months (a product default), both concluding Generally conforms. External assessments fall due every five years (MFMA Circular 65).

Periodic reports: Quarterly report to the Audit Committee (plan progress, significant findings, s32 totals, overdue actions with ageing, escalations, resource constraints, independence counts, conformance); Quarterly performance audit report (reg 14); Annual quality report. Each is issued only after its period ends and never changes.

The chair records noting (meeting date and minutes reference) only once the quarter's report is issued; a quarter not noted 60 days after it ends is overdue, and meetings are counted against four a year (MFMA s166).
operationalProcedures: 1. Manager or Head of Internal Audit: write the Engagement conclusion on the Report tab.
2. Preparers: record the Distribution list; Head of Internal Audit: Approve and issue final report.
3. Head of Internal Audit: record quality assessments on Quality programme.
4. Head of Internal Audit: on Periodic reports choose Prepare, write the narrative, then Issue.
5. Chair: Record noting on Workflow stages → Committee reports, and Record receipt on Quality programme.
takeaways: A report never claims conformance the quality programme does not support.
Issued means frozen: corrections are new versions, never edits.
No conclusion or distribution list, no final report.

quiz.question: The latest self-assessment concluded "Partially conforms". What does the next issued report say about conformance?
options: It states conformance with a footnote
It states conformance because the external assessment is current
It says conformance is not stated and lists the reasons
It leaves the section blank
quiz.explanation: The statement is printed only when the quality programme supports it; otherwise the reasons are listed.

quiz.question: Which of these is needed before Approve and issue final report?
options: A distribution list recorded for the report
The Audit Committee chair's noting
The Municipal Manager's acceptance of the report
An external quality assessment in the same year
quiz.explanation: The distribution list is a blocker of the issue step (Standard 15.1).

quiz.question: When can the chair record that the Committee noted a quarter's report?
options: At any time during the quarter
Only after the annual quality report is issued
Only after the Municipal Manager accepts it
Only once the Head of Internal Audit has issued that quarter's report
quiz.explanation: A quarter is noted only once its quarterly report is issued.

lessons.title: Follow-Up: Actions, Auditor-General Findings, Revised Dates and Escalations
lessons.subtitle: Stage 10: nothing closes until an independent auditor verifies it
lessons.overview: Follow-up tracks every management action to closure, for internal audit findings and, since MFMA s131 requires the municipality to address them, for findings of the Auditor-General too. Process owners start work, upload proof and submit remediation evidence; an auditor who is neither the owner nor the submitter verifies or rejects it; a manager or the Head of Internal Audit closes verified actions and then the finding. The follow-up register shows each action with its ageing, worked out from the current due date each time. A due date moves only through a recorded proposal that someone else decides, so the original stays on record. When management accepts a risk internal audit considers unacceptable, the Head of Internal Audit escalates it to the Audit Committee.
keyPoints: Ageing buckets: Not yet due, 0 to 30, 31 to 90, 91 to 180 and More than 180 days overdue (product defaults).

Auditor-General findings are recorded by audit managers or the Head of Internal Audit; their action plans are ordinary actions through the same evidence, verification and closure workflow, and process owners see those of their own department.

A revised due date is proposed by the action's owner with a reason and decided by an auditor, audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit in scope, never by the proposer; approval moves the due date and keeps the original.

Escalation sources: a risk acceptance at closure, a response that disagrees, or a finding left unremediated (offered when an action is more than 90 days overdue, a product default); nothing is escalated automatically.
An escalation notifies the Audit Committee chair and goes into the next quarterly report.
Close engagement needs every action verified or closed; otherwise the Head of Internal Audit records a risk acceptance with a reason.
operationalProcedures: 1. Process owner: open the action, Start work, Upload remediation evidence and Submit remediation evidence.
2. Auditor: Verify or Reject evidence with a reason.
3. Open Follow-up register and select an ageing tile to see what is late.
4. Record an Auditor-General finding and Add action for each item of management's plan.
5. Propose a revised date (owner) and Approve or Reject it (auditor in scope); escalate accepted risks from the Committee view.
takeaways: The person who submits evidence never verifies it.
A due date never moves silently: the original and every proposal stay visible.
Escalation is a judgement of the Head of Internal Audit, never automatic.

quiz.question: An action owner proposes a revised due date. Who may approve it?
options: The same owner, after a waiting period
An auditor, audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit in scope, other than the proposer
The Municipal Manager only
The Audit Committee chair only
quiz.explanation: action.due_date.decide belongs to internal audit in scope, and the proposer never decides their own.

quiz.question: How are Auditor-General findings' action plans handled?
options: As ordinary actions through the same evidence, verification and closure workflow
Outside the platform
By the Auditor-General in the platform
As internal audit findings with the 5 Cs
quiz.explanation: They are actions with source Auditor-General, sharing the action workflow.

quiz.question: A finding has an action 120 days overdue. What does the platform do about escalation?
options: Escalates it automatically to the Committee
Closes the finding as accepted risk
Notifies the Auditor-General
Offers it to the Head of Internal Audit as a candidate; nothing is escalated automatically
quiz.explanation: Findings with an action more than 90 days overdue are offered as possibly left unremediated; the Head of Internal Audit decides.

lessons.title: The Assistant, Controls over AI and Offline Work
lessons.subtitle: The assistant proposes, a named auditor takes responsibility, and the server decides
lessons.overview: The assistant answers questions from the records you may see, drafts text and proposes workflow steps, but it decides nothing: a proposal happens only when you confirm it, through the same checks as the button. Because AI-written content still has to be audit evidence, the platform labels it. Working papers, findings, audit evidence, the engagement conclusion, the report text and periodic report narratives carry an AI-assisted label, set by the system for content saved through the assistant and declared by a person for AI used outside the platform. Such an item is used as evidence, a finding or a conclusion only after a named auditor records an AI-content review at its current AI content version. By default the assistant is a local, rule-based engine and sends nothing out; an external model starts only with the operator's attestation that the provider contract excludes training on client data. Offline work follows the same principle: drafting works offline, deciding does not.
keyPoints: Every assistant answer lists its supporting records and labels each statement Evidence (read from a record), Inference (derived, saying how) or Uncertain. Citations are re-checked against the user's access; a record the user cannot open is treated as not existing.

A proposal shows what would change, what follows and whether it is allowed now. It can be confirmed once, within 15 minutes, only while the target record is unchanged; it is then carried out with every permission, segregation-of-duties and workflow check, and audited as done by the user through the assistant.
The AI-assisted label set by the system cannot be removed and an ordinary edit never clears it; a person may withdraw their own declaration.

The review statement is "I have reviewed the AI-assisted content of this item, verified it against the evidence, and take responsibility for it"; it is recorded by an auditor, audit manager or the Head of Internal Audit, never through the assistant. The preparer may review their own item (a product default to confirm).

Until reviewed: Mark as prepared and Submit for review are refused, the final report and a periodic report are not issued, and an AI-assisted conclusion is left out of the quarterly performance audit report. No override passes a missing review.
A later AI-assisted change (through the assistant, or a new or changed declaration) is a new AI content version and needs a new review; edits made without AI do not void it.

The AI register lists every AI-assisted item for the Head of Internal Audit; the Audit Committee chair sees counts only. Help & Training and the AI register state what is sent, to whom, and the training position.
The assistant reads and cites Auditor-General findings, escalations and periodic reports within your scope, and writes none of them.

Offline, users can draft working papers, record test results, draft and edit findings, draft management responses and capture evidence. Approvals, sign-offs, report issue, verification, closure, access, administration, exports, the assistant and report versions need a connection.

On reconnection the server re-checks session, role, scope, state, validation and version. A refused change comes back with the reason; a change drafted from an old version becomes a conflict that keeps both versions until a person chooses.
operationalProcedures: 1. Choose Assistant, ask in plain words naming records by id, and read Supporting records and the Evidence / Inference / Uncertain labels.
2. Ask for a step, read the proposal, and choose Confirm or Cancel.
3. Declare AI use under AI assistance when you used AI outside the platform.
4. As a named auditor, choose Record AI-content review after checking the item against its evidence.
5. Offline: open Offline work, draft, then Synchronise now on Sync status and resolve any conflicts.
takeaways: The assistant proposes; you decide.
AI-assisted content counts only after a named auditor takes responsibility for it.
No attestation, no external model: the local engine answers.

quiz.question: A working-paper section is added through a confirmed assistant proposal. What follows?
options: The paper is labelled AI-assisted and needs a named auditor's review before it can be marked prepared
Nothing; assistant content needs no review
The assistant marks the paper prepared
The section is deleted if not reviewed in 15 minutes
quiz.explanation: Content saved through the assistant is labelled by the system and must be reviewed at its current AI content version.

quiz.question: After a review is recorded, the preparer fixes a typo by hand without AI. What happens to the review?
options: It is voided
It moves to the Audit Committee
It stays; edits without AI do not void it
The AI label is removed
quiz.explanation: Only a later AI-assisted change creates a new AI content version that voids the review.

quiz.question: An external model is configured, but the operator has not recorded the no-training attestation. What answers questions?
options: The external model, with a warning
Nothing; the assistant is switched off
The external model, for the Head of Internal Audit only
The local engine; the external model is not started
quiz.explanation: Without the attestation the configuration falls back to the local engine.

lessons.title: Security, the Audit Trail and Operations
lessons.subtitle: Tamper-evident records, dual control, data protection and licensing
lessons.overview: The platform holds personal information about officials and opinions in findings, so its controls are built around POPIA, under which the municipality is the responsible party and Binteca, running the platform, is an operator. Every change, sign-in, administration step, export and download is written to a hash-chained audit trail that anyone with access can verify, and all data is encrypted at rest. Consequential operations are under dual control: privileged accounts, restores and disposals each need a second person. Security & Operations gives the IT administrator and the Head of Internal Audit backups and restore drills, the municipality's data exports, an incident register, access reviews, retention with legal hold, the end-of-contract exit and the licence.
keyPoints: The audit trail is hash-chained; Verify chain recomputes every hash and reports any edited, reordered or removed event. Individual reads are not logged.
Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, including the store, logs, evidence, exports, packages and backups.

Two-factor sign-in uses authenticator app codes with single-use recovery codes; another IT administrator resets a user's two-factor sign-in. Role changes, deactivations and resets end the user's sessions.
A restore is requested by the IT administrator and approved by the Head of Internal Audit; disposal under retention needs an approved request from a second person.

The municipality receives monthly data exports, quarterly delivery packages (the package key is shown to the Head of Internal Audit only) and, at the end of the contract, an exit package with a signed integrity statement, tracked against a 10-business-day deadline.

The incident register counts down 72 hours as the outer limit for notifying the municipality; the platform treats it as a limit, never a target, and the municipality notifies the Information Regulator.
Retention periods are set by the municipality (none by default); legal holds override disposal.

Licences are signed; unlicensed modules (data analytics, assistant, extraction, offline synchronisation) are refused by the server. An altered, expired or unsigned licence licenses nothing and never falls back to evaluation mode, which is labelled on every page.
The audit trail records every create, edit, sign-off and deletion with user and time, including every library change, override and AI-content review.
operationalProcedures: 1. Open Users & Roles and choose Issue account; privileged accounts go to a second person for approval.
2. Open Security & Ops → Access & two-factor to change roles, deactivate, reset MFA and approve waiting requests.
3. Open Offline devices and choose Revoke for a lost or retired device.
4. Open Audit Trail and choose Verify chain.
5. On Backups & restore choose Back up now, Verify or Restore drill; restores go through Request restore and Approve and restore.
6. Use Exports & deliveries, Incidents, Access reviews, Retention & legal hold and Exit (end of contract) as each situation requires.
takeaways: No one restores, disposes or issues a privileged account alone.
A verified hash chain is how you show the audit record has not been altered.
The 72-hour incident clock is the outer limit; notify sooner.

quiz.question: How does the platform treat the 72 hours in the incident register?
options: As the target time for notifying the municipality
As the time the Information Regulator allows for a fix
As the retention period for incident records
As the outer limit for notifying the municipality, never the target
quiz.explanation: The operator must notify the responsible party immediately; 72 hours is the outer limit, not a target.

quiz.question: Who takes part in restoring a backup?
options: The IT administrator alone
The IT administrator requests the restore and the Head of Internal Audit approves it
Any auditor with the Head of Internal Audit's approval
The Audit Committee
quiz.explanation: Restores are under dual control: the IT administrator requests and the Head of Internal Audit approves or rejects.

quiz.question: An installed licence file has been altered. What modules does it enable?
options: Every module, in evaluation mode
Only the modules not affected by the alteration
None; an altered licence licenses nothing and never falls back to evaluation
The modules of the previous licence
quiz.explanation: A licence that is altered, expired, not yet valid or unsigned licenses nothing, and it never falls back to evaluation mode.
